Riboﬂavin (vitamin B2)
Originally called vitamin G, riboﬂavin was renamed vitamin B2 when it was recognized to be part of the yeast B complex. The
cofactor forms for riboﬂavin are ﬂavin mononucleotide (FMN) and ﬂavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). Riboﬂavin is associated
with enzymes designated ﬂavoproteins. Riboﬂavin’s planar isoalloxazine ring facilitates the redox transfer reactions catalyzed by
FMN and FAD.
Functions
FMN is usually associated with membrane proteins involved in the mitochondrial electron system, whereas FAD is found in
membrane-bound and soluble enzymes. Flavins can exist in four redox states: the ﬂavin-N(5) oxide, quinone, semi-quinone,
and hydroquinone (Fig. 10A and B). FAD and FMN are cofactors usually used in aerobic processes, functioning as cofactors for
oxidases. However, FAD also can function in anaerobic environments as cofactor dehydrogenase reactions. Flavins are particularly
